html:
The Thule were the ancestors of the Inuit. Their culture took shape around the Bering Strait in western Alaska by about 1000 CE, and over the next two or three centuries they spread east across Arctic Canada to Greenland.

The Thule were expert sea hunters. They hunted bowhead whales from large open skin boats, the umiak, using harpoons with floats, and hunted seals and walrus from kayaks. Dogs pulled their sleds. They lived in winter houses dug into the ground and built of stone, turf and whale bone, and they used the bow and arrow.

The move east, the Thule migration, was fast. It may have followed the bowhead whales during a warm period, or the search for iron. In the eastern Arctic they met the older Dorset people, who disappeared not long after. In Greenland they met the Norse settlers, who called them Skraelings; Norse objects have turned up at Thule sites in the Canadian Arctic.

As the climate cooled in the Little Ice Age, Thule ways slowly turned into the many local cultures of the historic Inuit, from the Iñupiat of Alaska to the people of Greenland. Their relatives to the south in Alaska include the Yup'ik. The name comes from the Thule district of northwest Greenland, where their remains were first described, itself named after the far northern land of Greek legend.
sum: The Thule were the ancestors of the Inuit. Their culture took shape around the Bering Strait in western Alaska by about 1000 CE, and over the next two or three centuries they spread east across Arctic Canada to Greenland.
